blocks.text: Οἴνου δ᾽ ἐξέπιον κάδον, [Oinou d' exepion kadon,]
I drained a cadus of wine. And in the same place Hedylus in an Epigram,
Ἀλλὰ κάδοις Χίου με κατάβρεχε, [Alla kadois Chiou me katabreche,]
Here the translator ridiculously has But water by pouring wine from casks, instead of But drench me with casks of Chian wine [col. 44]: as in Tibullus, book 2, Elegy 1:
[II, 580] At what price shall we buy a cask of Chian? — — —

And like cabus, so cadus is of Hebrew origin. Just as קב kab is cabus, so כד cad is cadus, although the Hebrew כד has a wider range. For Moses, Solomon and Elijah use it for a water jar. See Gen. XXIV, 14. Eccles. XII, 8. and 1 Reg. XVIII, 34.

Having thus weighed the opinions of others, it now remains for us to put forward our own as well. To establish it, we must first lay down as most certain that by dove's dung some kind of food is meant. Otherwise there would be no coherence in this sentence: There was a great famine in Samaria: for an ass's head was sold for eighty pieces of silver, and the fourth part of a cab of dove's dung for five pieces of silver. Further, since it has been proved that dove's dung, as these words are commonly understood, is in no way a food, something else must necessarily be meant by them. When I consulted the Arabs on this matter, I found that two things are customarily marked with this epithet among them. One of them is what is called by another name كوز كندم [kūz kandum] kuz kendem, or جوز جندم [jawz jandum] giauz gendem, that is, a nut named after a place. For a nut is called كوز [kūz] kuz in Persian and جوز [jawz] giauz in Arabic. And Kendem or Gendem is the same word, for the Persian Caph there sounds as G because of the three dots placed over it. Of this nut Avicenna, book 2 of the Canon, says: كوز كندم الماهية هو خفيف كالاشنة طيني وبالرقة يسمونه حرا الحمام وببغداد يسمي جوز جندم الاختيار اجوده المربري والذفني ضغيف [kūz kandum al-māhiyya huwa khafīf ka-l-ushna ṭīnī wa-bi-l-Raqqa yusammūnahu ḥurā al-ḥamām wa-bi-Baghdād yusammā jawz jandum al-ikhtiyār ajwaduhu al-mrbrī wa-l-dhfnī ḍghīf] Kuzkendem, what is it? It is a light thing, like tree moss, clay-like. In the city of Raqqa (on the Euphrates below Samosata in Mesopotamia) they call it dove's dung. And in Baghdad giauz Gendem. Selection: the best is the Barbaric, but the Daphnensian is weak. See the rest there. The same author elsewhere: جوز جندم الطبع قال بولس له قوة مبردة مطفية مجففة قليلا [jawz jandum al-ṭabʿ qāla Būlus lahu quwwa mubarrida muṭfiya mujaffifa qalīlan] Giauz, or the nut Gendem. Its nature. Paul said that it has the power of cooling, quenching and drying somewhat. But the definition is omitted there; in the Latin version it reads thus: What is the nut Kendem? It is a granular earth like a chickpea, white, inclining to yellow, which is exported from Barca and from Corascena, from which wine is made with honey. If this definition is true, it does not help us at all. For it is a kind of earth, and no kind of earth is edible.
